stem: A developer suspects their application's JSON parsing code (not the model itself) is the source of a bug. What is a direct way to test this specific hypothesis?
explanation: Feeding the parsing code a manually-constructed, known-valid sample JSON string (bypassing the model entirely) and checking whether the parsing code handles it correctly tests this specific hypothesis directly, isolating the parsing logic from any potential variability in the model's actual output, letting the developer confirm or rule out the parsing code itself as the source of the bug.
reference: Testing parsing code in isolation from the model

choices.text: Feeding the parsing code a manually-constructed, known-valid sample JSON string (bypassing the model entirely).
choices.reasoning: Correct: this is the direct, isolating diagnostic technique for exactly this hypothesis, testing the parsing code independently confirms or rules out the code itself as the bug's source, separate from any potential model-output variability.

choices.text: There is no way to test this hypothesis without also involving the model in every single test.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this dismisses a real, practical isolation technique (testing the parsing logic with a manually constructed sample, independent of the model) for exactly this diagnostic purpose.

choices.text: This can only be tested by switching to a different model tier.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is a code-isolation debugging technique, not something addressed by changing which model tier is used.

choices.text: This hypothesis can only be confirmed by contacting Anthropic support directly.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is something the developer can and should test directly themselves through isolated code testing, without needing outside support.

stem: A developer building a customer-facing feature wants their evaluation set to include not just typical, common inputs but also known tricky edge cases (very short inputs, ambiguous phrasing, unusual formatting). Why is this deliberate inclusion of edge cases important, connecting to a principle discussed for few-shot examples?
explanation: This connects to the same representativeness principle discussed for few-shot examples, an evaluation set composed only of easy, typical cases won't reveal how the system actually handles the harder, edge-case scenarios it will genuinely encounter in real-world usage, so deliberately including known tricky cases gives a more complete, realistic picture of actual system reliability across the full range of inputs it needs to handle, not just the easy majority.
reference: Deliberately including edge cases, connecting to few-shot representativeness principle

choices.text: The same representativeness principle discussed for few-shot examples.
choices.reasoning: Correct: this connects the evaluation-set-composition principle to the same representativeness reasoning discussed for few-shot example selection, both benefit from deliberately covering the genuine range of cases (including tricky ones) rather than only the easy, typical majority.

choices.text: There is no benefit to including edge cases in an evaluation set; only typical, common inputs provide any useful evaluation signal.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this dismisses the real, meaningful value of testing against genuinely tricky cases, which reveals reliability characteristics that testing only easy, typical cases would completely miss.

choices.text: This consideration only applies if the feature uses extended thinking.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: the value of including representative edge cases in an evaluation set applies broadly, independent of whether extended thinking happens to be used.

choices.text: This can only be achieved by switching to a different model tier.
choices.reasoning: Incorrect: this is an evaluation-set-composition/design practice, not something addressed by changing which model tier is used.
